questions.stem: What is the difference between respiration and breathing?

options.text: Respiration is a chemical process that releases energy from glucose in cells; breathing is the mechanical movement of air in and out of the lungs
Breathing is the chemical process; respiration is the mechanical process
Respiration only occurs in the lungs; breathing occurs in all cells
They are the same process

questions.explanation: Respiration is a chemical process that takes place in every living cell — it releases energy from glucose to make ATP. Breathing (ventilation) is the physical movement of air in and out of the lungs. They are NOT the same thing. This confusion is one of the most common misconceptions in biology.

questions.stem: Do plants carry out cellular respiration?

options.text: Yes — all living cells respire, including plant cells
Yes — but only at night when they cannot photosynthesise
No — plants only photosynthesise
No — only animals respire

questions.explanation: ALL living cells respire, including plant cells, fungal cells, and bacterial cells. Plants respire 24 hours a day in all their cells. During the day, they also photosynthesise, but this does not replace respiration. Respiration is essential for providing ATP for cellular processes.

questions.stem: Where does glycolysis take place?

options.text: On the cell membrane
In the cytoplasm
In the mitochondria
In the nucleus

questions.explanation: Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm, not in the mitochondria. It is the first stage of both aerobic and anaerobic respiration. Glucose (6C) is split into two molecules of pyruvate (3C), with a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 reduced NAD. Since it occurs in the cytoplasm, it can happen in all cells, including prokaryotes that lack mitochondria.

questions.stem: What is the word equation for aerobic respiration?

options.text: Glucose → Ethanol + Carbon dioxide + Energy
Glucose + Oxygen → Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy (ATP)
Carbon dioxide + Water → Glucose + Oxygen
Glucose → Lactic acid + Energy

questions.explanation: The word equation for aerobic respiration is: Glucose + Oxygen → Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy (released as ATP). This is the reverse of photosynthesis. Option C is anaerobic respiration in animals; option D is anaerobic respiration in yeast.

questions.stem: What is the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain during aerobic respiration?

options.text: Carbon dioxide
Oxygen
NADH
Glucose

questions.explanation: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain. It combines with hydrogen ions (H⁺) and electrons to form water. This is why aerobic respiration requires oxygen. Without oxygen, the electron transport chain stops, and the cell must rely on anaerobic respiration.

questions.stem: Where does the Krebs cycle take place?

options.text: On the inner mitochondrial membrane
In the nucleus
In the cytoplasm
In the mitochondrial matrix

questions.explanation: The Krebs cycle (citric acid cycle) takes place in the mitochondrial matrix. Here, acetyl CoA is broken down, releasing CO₂ and producing reduced NAD, reduced FAD, and a small amount of ATP via substrate-level phosphorylation. The link reaction (pyruvate → acetyl CoA) also occurs in the matrix.

questions.stem: Where does the electron transport chain (oxidative phosphorylation) take place?

options.text: On the inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae)
On the outer mitochondrial membrane
In the cytoplasm
In the mitochondrial matrix

questions.explanation: The electron transport chain is located on the inner mitochondrial membrane, which is folded into cristae to increase surface area. Electrons from reduced NAD and reduced FAD pass along the chain, pumping H⁺ ions across the membrane. The flow of H⁺ back through ATP synthase produces most of the ATP (chemiosmosis).

questions.stem: What are the products of anaerobic respiration in human muscle cells?

options.text: Lactic acid and carbon dioxide
Carbon dioxide and water
Lactic acid only
Ethanol and carbon dioxide

questions.explanation: In human muscle cells, anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid only (no CO₂). In yeast and plants, anaerobic respiration (fermentation) produces ethanol and CO₂. This is a key distinction that students often confuse. The build-up of lactic acid causes muscle fatigue and pain.

questions.stem: What are the products of anaerobic respiration in yeast?

options.text: Water and ATP only
Ethanol and carbon dioxide
Lactic acid only
Glucose and oxygen

questions.explanation: In yeast (and plant cells under anaerobic conditions), anaerobic respiration produces ethanol (alcohol) and carbon dioxide. This process is called alcoholic fermentation and is used in brewing (beer, wine) and baking (CO₂ makes bread rise). In animals, lactic acid is produced instead.

questions.stem: How much ATP does glycolysis produce per molecule of glucose (net gain)?

options.text: 0 ATP
4 ATP
2 ATP
36 ATP

questions.explanation: Glycolysis produces a net gain of 2 ATP per glucose molecule. Although 4 ATP are produced, 2 ATP are used in the initial phosphorylation steps, giving a net gain of 2. Glycolysis also produces 2 molecules of reduced NAD and 2 molecules of pyruvate.

questions.stem: Which stage of aerobic respiration produces the most ATP?

options.text: Oxidative phosphorylation (electron transport chain)
The Krebs cycle
The link reaction
Glycolysis

questions.explanation: Oxidative phosphorylation (the electron transport chain and chemiosmosis) produces the vast majority of ATP — approximately 26-28 ATP per glucose molecule. This is far more than glycolysis (2 ATP), the link reaction (0 ATP directly), or the Krebs cycle (2 ATP via substrate-level phosphorylation).

questions.stem: Why is the actual ATP yield from aerobic respiration (approximately 30-32 ATP) lower than the theoretical maximum (38 ATP)?

options.text: Because oxygen is never fully available
Because the enzymes are always partially denatured
Due to proton leakage across the membrane and the energy cost of transporting molecules into the mitochondria
Because some glucose is always converted to fat

questions.explanation: The actual ATP yield is lower than the theoretical maximum because: (1) some protons leak across the inner mitochondrial membrane without passing through ATP synthase, (2) energy is used to actively transport pyruvate, NADH, and ADP into/out of the mitochondria, and (3) NADH produced in the cytoplasm requires a shuttle system to enter mitochondria.

questions.stem: What happens to pyruvate in the link reaction?

options.text: It is split into glucose and oxygen
It is converted to acetyl CoA, with CO₂ and reduced NAD produced
It is converted to lactic acid
It is directly used by the electron transport chain

questions.explanation: In the link reaction, pyruvate (3C) is decarboxylated (a CO₂ molecule is removed) and combined with coenzyme A to form acetyl CoA (2C). NAD is reduced to NADH. This reaction occurs in the mitochondrial matrix and links glycolysis to the Krebs cycle.

questions.stem: What is the role of NAD and FAD in respiration?

options.text: They are waste products of respiration
They are substrates that are broken down for energy
They are hydrogen/electron carriers that transfer hydrogen to the electron transport chain
They are enzymes that catalyse the reactions

questions.explanation: NAD and FAD are coenzymes that act as hydrogen (electron) carriers. During glycolysis, the link reaction, and the Krebs cycle, they are reduced (NAD → NADH, FAD → FADH₂) by accepting hydrogen atoms. They then carry these to the electron transport chain, where the electrons are used to generate ATP.

questions.stem: Does glycolysis require oxygen?

options.text: No — but it requires carbon dioxide
Yes — oxygen is needed for all stages of respiration
Yes — but only in animal cells
No — glycolysis is anaerobic and occurs in both aerobic and anaerobic respiration

questions.explanation: Glycolysis does NOT require oxygen. It is an anaerobic process that occurs in the cytoplasm of all cells. It is the first stage of both aerobic and anaerobic respiration. If oxygen is available, pyruvate enters the mitochondria for aerobic respiration. If not, anaerobic pathways are used instead.

questions.stem: What is ATP?

options.text: A sugar that is broken down during respiration
Adenosine triphosphate — the universal energy currency of cells
A type of lipid that stores energy
A type of protein used for muscle contraction

questions.explanation: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is a nucleotide that acts as the universal energy currency in all living cells. When ATP is hydrolysed to ADP + Pi (inorganic phosphate), energy is released for cellular processes such as muscle contraction, active transport, and protein synthesis.

questions.stem: Where is CO₂ released during aerobic respiration?

options.text: Only during glycolysis
During the electron transport chain when oxygen accepts electrons
CO₂ is not produced during respiration
During the link reaction and the Krebs cycle (decarboxylation reactions)

questions.explanation: CO₂ is released during decarboxylation reactions in the link reaction (pyruvate → acetyl CoA) and the Krebs cycle. It is NOT produced during glycolysis or the electron transport chain. Oxygen is consumed at the ETC as the final electron acceptor, forming water — not CO₂.

questions.stem: Why does aerobic respiration produce much more ATP than anaerobic respiration?

options.text: Because in aerobic respiration, the electron transport chain uses reduced NAD and FAD to generate large amounts of ATP via oxidative phosphorylation
Because anaerobic respiration uses a different type of glucose
Because anaerobic respiration requires more ATP to start
Because aerobic respiration occurs faster

questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration produces ~30-32 ATP per glucose compared to only 2 ATP from anaerobic respiration. This is because the Krebs cycle and link reaction produce many molecules of reduced NAD and FAD, which donate electrons to the electron transport chain, driving oxidative phosphorylation. Without oxygen, these stages cannot occur.

questions.stem: What is oxygen debt (excess post-exercise oxygen consumption)?

options.text: The amount of CO₂ produced during exercise
The oxygen stored in the lungs during exercise
The amount of oxygen used during exercise
The extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down the lactic acid that accumulated during anaerobic respiration

questions.explanation: Oxygen debt (EPOC) is the extra oxygen the body needs after vigorous exercise to metabolise the lactic acid that built up during anaerobic respiration. Lactic acid is transported in the blood to the liver, where it is converted back to glucose (requiring oxygen). This is why you continue to breathe heavily after exercise stops.

questions.stem: What is chemiosmosis?

options.text: The flow of H⁺ ions down their concentration gradient through ATP synthase, driving ATP production
The breakdown of glucose into pyruvate
The active transport of glucose into cells
The diffusion of chemicals across a membrane

questions.explanation: Chemiosmosis is the process by which the flow of hydrogen ions (protons, H⁺) down their concentration gradient through ATP synthase enzyme drives the synthesis of ATP from ADP + Pi. The H⁺ gradient is created by the electron transport chain pumping H⁺ from the matrix into the intermembrane space.

questions.stem: What is substrate-level phosphorylation?

options.text: The production of ATP by the electron transport chain
The phosphorylation of glucose at the start of glycolysis
The direct transfer of a phosphate group from a substrate to ADP to form ATP, without the electron transport chain
The addition of phosphate to NAD

questions.explanation: Substrate-level phosphorylation is the direct transfer of a phosphate group from a phosphorylated intermediate to ADP, forming ATP. It occurs during glycolysis and the Krebs cycle. This is different from oxidative phosphorylation, which uses the electron transport chain and chemiosmosis to produce ATP.

questions.stem: Which respiratory substrate yields the most energy per gram?

options.text: Proteins
All substrates yield the same energy per gram
Carbohydrates
Lipids (fats)

questions.explanation: Lipids yield approximately 39 kJ per gram, compared to about 17 kJ per gram for carbohydrates and 17 kJ per gram for proteins. This is because lipids have a higher proportion of hydrogen atoms (and therefore more electrons to pass through the electron transport chain), and they contain less oxygen than carbohydrates.

questions.stem: What is the respiratory quotient (RQ)?

options.text: The ratio of CO₂ produced to O₂ consumed
The total amount of oxygen used during respiration
The rate of breathing per minute
The amount of glucose used per hour

questions.explanation: The respiratory quotient (RQ) is calculated as: RQ = CO₂ produced ÷ O₂ consumed. For carbohydrates, RQ = 1.0. For lipids, RQ ≈ 0.7. For proteins, RQ ≈ 0.8. An RQ greater than 1.0 suggests anaerobic respiration is occurring (producing CO₂ without consuming O₂).

questions.stem: What is the RQ value when glucose is the respiratory substrate?
questions.explanation: When glucose is respired aerobically, the RQ = 1.0 because equal amounts of CO₂ are produced and O₂ are consumed: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O. RQ = 6CO₂/6O₂ = 1.0. A lower RQ (e.g., 0.7 for fats) means more O₂ is consumed relative to CO₂ produced.

questions.stem: How does exercise affect the rate of respiration?

options.text: Exercise has no effect on respiration
Exercise increases respiration rate because muscles need more ATP for contraction
Exercise only increases anaerobic respiration, never aerobic
Exercise decreases respiration rate

questions.explanation: During exercise, muscles contract more frequently and with greater force, requiring more ATP. To produce this ATP, the rate of respiration increases. Heart rate and breathing rate increase to deliver more oxygen and glucose to muscles and remove more CO₂. During intense exercise, anaerobic respiration also increases.

questions.stem: Why do mitochondria have a folded inner membrane (cristae)?

options.text: To store more DNA
To prevent oxygen from entering
To reduce the volume of the matrix
To increase the surface area for the electron transport chain and ATP synthase enzymes

questions.explanation: The cristae (folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane) greatly increase the surface area available for the electron transport chain proteins and ATP synthase enzymes. More surface area means more sites for oxidative phosphorylation, allowing more ATP to be produced. Cells that need lots of energy (like muscle cells) have mitochondria with more cristae.

questions.stem: What happens to lactic acid after exercise?

options.text: It is converted to ethanol in the muscles
It is permanently stored in the muscles
It is transported to the liver and converted back to glucose
It is exhaled from the lungs

questions.explanation: After exercise, lactic acid is transported in the blood to the liver, where it is converted back to glucose (this requires oxygen — part of the oxygen debt). Some glucose may be stored as glycogen in the liver. Lactic acid is not permanently stored, exhaled, or converted to ethanol in humans.

questions.stem: What is the balanced chemical equation for aerobic respiration?

options.text: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy (ATP)
6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂
C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃

questions.explanation: The balanced equation for aerobic respiration is: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy (ATP). Option B is photosynthesis (the reverse). Option C is alcoholic fermentation in yeast. Option D represents lactic acid fermentation.

questions.stem: A respirometer measures oxygen consumption. If cyanide (an ETC inhibitor) is added to the experiment, what happens?

options.text: Oxygen consumption drops to near zero because the electron transport chain is blocked
Oxygen consumption increases dramatically
CO₂ production increases but O₂ consumption is unchanged
Oxygen consumption stays the same because glycolysis continues

questions.explanation: Cyanide blocks the electron transport chain by inhibiting cytochrome c oxidase (the final electron carrier). This prevents electrons from being passed to oxygen, so oxygen is no longer consumed. The Krebs cycle also stops because reduced NAD and FAD cannot be recycled. Only glycolysis can continue (anaerobically).

questions.stem: How many molecules of pyruvate are produced from one molecule of glucose during glycolysis?
questions.explanation: One molecule of glucose (a 6-carbon compound) is split into two molecules of pyruvate (each a 3-carbon compound) during glycolysis. This means the Krebs cycle turns twice for every glucose molecule, and the link reaction occurs twice per glucose.

questions.stem: Why is anaerobic respiration less efficient than aerobic respiration?

options.text: Because glucose is not fully oxidised — the products (lactic acid or ethanol) still contain chemical energy
Because anaerobic respiration produces more heat
Because anaerobic respiration uses more glucose
Because anaerobic respiration only occurs in plant cells

questions.explanation: Anaerobic respiration is less efficient because glucose is only partially broken down — the products (lactic acid or ethanol) still contain a lot of chemical energy that has not been released. Only 2 ATP per glucose are produced (from glycolysis alone) compared to ~30-32 ATP from aerobic respiration.

questions.stem: In the Krebs cycle, what happens to the acetyl group from acetyl CoA?

options.text: It is stored as glycogen
It is directly converted to ATP
It combines with a 4-carbon compound (oxaloacetate) and is gradually broken down, releasing CO₂ and producing reduced NAD and FAD
It is converted back to pyruvate

questions.explanation: In the Krebs cycle, the 2-carbon acetyl group from acetyl CoA combines with the 4-carbon compound oxaloacetate to form a 6-carbon compound (citrate). Through a series of reactions, two carbon atoms are removed as CO₂, and the 4-carbon oxaloacetate is regenerated. Along the way, reduced NAD, reduced FAD, and ATP are produced.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of fermentation in yeast?

options.text: To produce oxygen for the yeast to breathe
To produce glucose for the yeast to store
To break down ethanol into water
To regenerate NAD so that glycolysis can continue when oxygen is unavailable

questions.explanation: The main purpose of fermentation is to regenerate NAD (by oxidising NADH back to NAD). NAD is needed as a hydrogen acceptor in glycolysis. Without oxygen, the electron transport chain cannot accept electrons from NADH, so fermentation provides an alternative way to recycle NAD, allowing glycolysis to continue producing 2 ATP per glucose.

questions.stem: A student says 'during respiration, oxygen is converted into carbon dioxide.' Why is this incorrect?

options.text: Because respiration does not involve any gases
Because oxygen is only used in photosynthesis, not respiration
Because oxygen and CO₂ have different fates — O₂ is the final electron acceptor forming water, while CO₂ is released from decarboxylation of carbon compounds
Because CO₂ is converted into oxygen, not the other way around

questions.explanation: Oxygen is NOT converted into CO₂. They come from different sources and have different roles: O₂ is the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain and combines with H⁺ to form water. CO₂ is produced when carbon atoms are removed from substrates (decarboxylation) during the link reaction and Krebs cycle.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of anaerobic respiration?

options.text: It can provide ATP quickly when oxygen supply is insufficient, such as during intense exercise
It completely breaks down glucose, releasing all the stored energy
It produces no waste products
It produces more ATP per glucose than aerobic respiration

questions.explanation: The main advantage of anaerobic respiration is that it can produce ATP quickly without needing oxygen. During intense exercise, when oxygen cannot be delivered fast enough to muscles, anaerobic respiration supplements the ATP supply. However, it produces only 2 ATP per glucose (less efficient) and creates lactic acid as a by-product.
